analysis.one_liner: Funds health studies and community grants at hazardous waste sites and forces owners to reduce risky exposures.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: after its March 1992 introduction with 28 Democratic cosponsors, it sat in a subcommittee and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let the federal Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry run health studies at hazardous waste sites, and when a study found exposure that could endanger health, it would have required the EPA or the state to order the facility's owner to reduce that exposure. It would have given people living near these sites advance notice, public meetings, a chance to comment, the right to petition for a study, and small grants to hire their own health experts. It also would have charged the facility owners for those community grants and pushed EPA to test alternatives to burning hazardous waste.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near hazardous waste sites, especially the communities around the 25 sites deemed highest-risk: they would get advance notice of studies, public meetings, copies of findings, the right to petition for a study, and grants of up to $50,000 to hire epidemiologists or toxicologists to interpret government findings for them. If a study found potentially dangerous exposure, the facility owner would be legally required to reduce it.

how_it_helps.text: The Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry could conduct health studies at any covered hazardous waste facility, and if a study found exposure that may present a health risk, the EPA or the state would have to order the owner or operator to reduce the exposure and eliminate or substantially mitigate the risk.

Residents would get real notice and a voice: newspapers ads before any study, a public meeting on the study's design, 30-day comment periods, a copy of the finished report on request, and a public meeting to explain the results.
Any person could petition for a health study, and the agency would have to answer within 120 days and explain in writing why it declined.

Community groups could receive health education grants of up to $50,000 to hire health professionals to explain exposure threats, review government studies, help write public comments, and design community health surveillance — with the 10 percent match waived for low-income communities.
The cost of those grants could be recovered from the facility owner as a condition of its permit and as a cleanup cost under the Superfund law from the parties that caused the contamination.
The agency would have had to complete health assessments at the 25 facilities believed to pose the highest risk to human health by July 1993 and report to Congress on the exposure and needed fixes.

New boards would check the work: a scientific Peer Review Board and a Citizen Review Board of people who live near waste sites to monitor how responsive the agencies are to community concerns and how readable their documents are.

The bill would fund demonstrations of non-incineration technologies for treating dioxin and hazardous waste, and require EPA to consider those alternatives in cleanup decisions — relevant to communities near incinerators.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of hazardous waste facilities, who would face mandatory exposure-reduction orders, could be billed for the community education grants as a condition of keeping their permits, and could see cleanup costs rise as EPA considers alternatives to incineration. Taxpayers would fund the program: $5 million a year for the health studies for fiscal 1993 through 1998, up to $500,000 a year for the Citizen Review Board, and about $1.5 million for the technology demonstrations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hazardous waste facility owners and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Cleanup orders would be triggered by a finding that exposure 'may present a potential risk' — a lower threshold than proof of harm — so facility owners could face expensive mandated remediation on uncertain science, and those costs would tend to flow into waste disposal prices.

The required notice, public meetings, and 30-day comment periods before and after each study could slow health assessments and cleanup decisions, though the bill does let the agency suspend those comment periods when needed to protect public health.
The program depends on yearly appropriations of at least $5 million plus board and grant funding, which Congress could decline to provide even if the bill became law.

The help to residents is modest in scale: grants are capped at $50,000 per facility group, one grant per facility, and each group must put up a 10 percent match unless it is low-income or already has a Superfund technical assistance grant.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the communities living next to the nation's most dangerous waste sites, the benefits — mandatory responses to documented exposure, independent technical help, and a formal voice in studies — clearly outweighed a program costing a few million dollars a year, much of it recoverable from the polluters themselves. The main honest concerns are process: the 'potential risk' trigger for mandatory cleanup orders could impose large costs on owners based on incomplete science, and the public-comment steps could add months to assessments. The bill also left itself exposed to Congress simply refusing to appropriate the money.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 1992, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up again before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Gephardt introduced the bill on March 25, 1992, joined by Reps. Richardson, Markey, Towns, and Waxman, and it gathered 28 Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and on April 3, 1992 to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials.
No hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed; the bill's record ends with the subcommittee referral, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and operators of hazardous waste facilities were better off, because they never faced the mandated exposure-reduction orders, permit-based charges for community grants, or a push toward alternatives to incineration. Communities near the highest-risk sites got none of the promised health assessments or technical assistance.

for.name: Rep. Richard Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and lined up original cosponsors including Reps. Richardson, Markey, Towns, and Waxman.

for.name: 28 of 267 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and referred it to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials on April 3, 1992; the committee never reported the bill out or scheduled action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 recorded supporters — the sponsor and 28 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and no vote ever took place that would show how anyone else would have lined up.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facilities
industries.note: Facility owners would face mandatory orders to reduce exposures found by health studies, could be billed for community education grants as a condition of their permits, and could have grant costs charged to them as Superfund response costs. Their interest in avoiding those obligations ran directly against residents' interest in knowing and reducing exposure.

The bill would fund demonstrations of non-incineration treatment technologies for dioxin and hazardous waste and require EPA to consider those alternatives in cleanup decisions, putting the first public money behind a competitor to burning waste.

industries.industry: Environmental consulting and health research firms
industries.note: The bill would fund health studies, data collection that can be contracted to universities and private firms, community technical assistance, and technology demonstration grants — new paid work for epidemiologists, toxicologists, and remediation specialists.
